title: The Warehouse Out Back

post.author: u/gate_code_briallen
post.title: I do nights at a self-storage place. A tenant's lease ended, her unit was cleared and let to someone else, and for seven days a link in her family chat still showed it full of her things.

blocks.text: I'm the night manager at Prothero Self Storage: 212 units, one gate, and me. Our app lets tenants photograph and film their units and share an album with a link. Ifor Noakes, who built it, keeps the photos and videos with a cloud storage provider, a company that rents out space for files. The leases live in the app's database, the program that keeps its records.

Sharing is quick. The tenant taps Share. The app makes a link to each file and hands them back. She posts them wherever she likes. Ifor set every share link to last 7 days, the longest the provider allows, so that links never break.

Mrs Anwen Kittredge rented C-14 for nineteen years. Her lease ended at midnight on Tuesday 22 September. On Wednesday the crew cleared C-14 at 10:00, and at 16:00 we let it to a Mr Haskard. At midnight on Wednesday, a day after her lease ended, Mrs Kittredge opened our app, which still let her in, and shared her C-14 album in her family chat: 38 photos and 2 videos.

That Wednesday at 21:00 Mr Haskard filmed his new unit for his insurer and tried to upload it, sending it from his phone to our storage, from the yard, where the signal comes and goes. The video was 612 MiB; Ifor's app counts in MiB, mebibytes of 1,048,576 bytes. It failed at 90 percent and started again from zero. Four times.
On Wednesday 30 September at 23:40 her grandson came to the gate and held up his phone. C-14, full. Her late husband's armchair facing the door. The boxes labelled in her hand. The lamp, switched on.
The armchair went to a charity shop a week ago. The lamp went in a skip.
We walked down row C. Mr Haskard's padlock on C-14. Through the vent, his boxes. On the phone, her chair. Ifor sent me his logs.

Each line shows the day and time, what it's about, the unit, the tenant where there is one, and what happened. The bucket is the storage space at the provider that holds our files. GET means a phone asked for them; 200 OK means they were sent, and 403 Forbidden means refused:

Wed 23 Sep 00:00  lease   C-14  KITTREDGE  ended
Wed 23 Sep 10:00  unit    C-14  cleared
Wed 23 Sep 16:00  lease   C-14  HASKARD  started
Wed 23 Sep 21:38  upload  C-14  HASKARD  attempt 4 failed at 551 of 612 MiB (90%), gave up
Thu 24 Sep 00:00  share   C-14  KITTREDGE  40 files, link expires Thu 01 Oct 00:00
Thu 24 Sep 00:02  bucket  GET units/C-14/  200 OK
                  12 opens, all 200 OK, the last Wed 30 Sep 23:40
Thu 01 Oct 00:20  bucket  GET units/C-14/  403 Forbidden  link expired

He opened it once more at 00:20, outside C-14: 403 Forbidden. Eight days after her lease ended, the link stopped. For the seven days before that, it showed a room that wasn't there. The owner says delete everything the day a lease ends. Ifor says the storage never asked anyone about the lease. Painted inside the gate office:

blocks.title: RULE OF THE YARD
items: WHEN A LEASE ENDS, EVERY KEY COMES BACK.
A KEY YOU CANNOT FIND IS STILL IN SOMEONE'S HAND.

blocks.label: ifor_share_c14.png

diagram.aria: Ifor's drawing of the C-14 share. Wednesday 23 September at 00:00 the database records that Mrs Kittredge's lease ended, and at 16:00 that C-14 was let again. At 00:00 on Thursday her phone asks the Prothero app to share the C-14 album. The app checks only her login and returns a link that expires in 7 days, without asking the database. She posts it in the family chat. The family chat opens it 12 times from Thursday 00:02 to Wednesday 30 September 23:40, and the bucket answers 200 OK with C-14 full each time. On Thursday 1 October at 00:20 the bucket answers 403 Forbidden: the link expired.

blocks.caption: Ifor's drawing of the C-14 share. The database knew the lease ended at 00:00 on Wednesday and that C-14 was let again at 16:00. At 00:00 on Thursday the app checked only that Mrs Kittredge was logged in and handed her a link that expired in 7 days. Nothing asked the database. The family chat opened it 12 times, the last at 23:40 on Wednesday 30 September, and the bucket showed C-14 full every time. At 00:20 on Thursday 1 October it said 403 Forbidden.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your provider is object storage. A bucket holds objects. Each object is one whole file stored under a key, its name, such as units/C-14/IMG_0412.jpg. It is written and read whole over HTTP, the web's request language. There are no real folders, only keys that look like paths. Ifor's share link is a presigned URL: a web address with a permission slip built in. It works in steps. First the app signs the link, stamping it with a signature made from its secret credentials, its login to the provider, and an expiry time. Then whoever holds the link sends it to the bucket. The bucket checks that the signature is genuine and the time hasn't passed, and if both hold, sends the file. Now your log. When was the C-14 link signed, and what did the app look up before signing it? Once it was in the family chat, which part of your system knew the lease had ended, and did anything ask it? What would it have taken to stop that link before Thursday? And Mr Haskard's video: when the signal dropped at 551 MiB, what did the bucket keep?

replies.author: u/gate_code_briallen
replies.text: Ifor says the app signs with one long-lived access key, a secret that works until someone switches it off. It belongs to an IAM user, a named login in the provider's account system; IAM is short for Identity and Access Management. So the 7 days always hold. And the app checks you're logged in, not whether your lease is current. Each unit has a gallery page in the app that only its tenant can open; sharing skips it and hands out links to the files. He says it isn't the first time. On Thursday 24 September at 18:00 Ms Senna Quist in A-03 shared her album with a removal man, who opened it at 19:30. She withdrew the share in the app on Friday at 12:00, after he was let go. The log shows him opening it again on Saturday at 02:10 and on Monday at 03:30.

comments.author: u/never_expire_zennor
comments.text: Links that expire annoy customers. Every expired link is a support ticket and a tenant who thinks your app is broken. Make the bucket public. A public bucket lets anyone read an object by its plain web address, with no signature and nothing to expire, so the links work forever. They're photos of boxes in a shed. Nobody is guessing unit numbers at two in the morning, and if a lease ends you can tidy up then.

replies.author: u/grey_pager
replies.text: Whose names are written on those boxes? And what would a public bucket have done about Ms Quist's removal man on Saturday at 02:10?

comments.author: u/resume_from_tegid
comments.text: On the video: a single upload is one request, so if the signal drops at 90 percent the bucket keeps nothing and the app starts again. Object storage will also take a file as a multipart upload, in three steps. You start it. You send numbered parts, and each can be retried on its own. Then you ask the bucket to join them into one object. Parts you never finish still sit there and are billed until you stop the upload, though. And decide whether the bytes go through your own server, the computer that runs your app, or straight from the phone to the bucket with a presigned upload link: one signed to allow sending a file instead of reading one.

replies.author: u/gate_code_briallen
replies.text: Ifor says the yard's signal holds for about 551 MiB at Mr Haskard's 1 MiB a second, then drops for about 30 seconds. The video is 4 minutes 16 seconds long. Once videos go in, he wants a chain of steps. When a file lands, the bucket sends an event, a short message, to a queue, a to-do list. A worker, a helper program, picks it up and transcodes the video: it makes new copies at different sizes and bitrates, the bits of data used per second of video. He'd make 4 variant streams, 1080p, 720p, 480p and 360p, from sharpest to smallest. Each is cut into 6-second segments, small files, listed in a playlist. That's how HLS, HTTP Live Streaming, works, so a phone on weak signal can drop to a smaller one. He also says our busiest hour, 19:00 to 20:00, is about 400 gallery opens of about 120 MiB each. A page and its links alone are about 0.05 MiB. And the app server has a 100 Mbps line: 100 million bits a second.

reply.prompt: The next lease ends on Friday, and Mr Haskard wants to try his video again. What should Ifor change first? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Share a gallery page that checks the lease and signs 5-minute links each visit, and upload video in 8 MiB parts.
options.part2: Ifor made a share a link to the unit's gallery page. Each time it opens, the app asks the database whether this person may see these files now, and only then signs links that last 5 minutes. Videos go up straight from the phone as multipart uploads in 8 MiB parts. We replayed the week. At midnight on Thursday Mrs Kittredge tapped Share on C-14; the app asked the database, found her lease had ended at 00:00 on Wednesday, and made no link. Nothing went into the family chat. Ms Quist's removal man opened her gallery at 19:30 on Thursday; after she withdrew the share on Friday, his opens at 02:10 on Saturday and 03:30 on Monday were refused. No open that should have been refused got through, and no rightful one was turned away. Mr Haskard's signal dropped at 551 MiB with parts 1 to 68 already stored; only part 69 went again, and the upload finished at 21:10:49 with 7 MiB thrown away. In the busiest hour the app server sent about 20 MiB of pages and links. On Wednesday 30 September at 23:40 nobody came to the gate. I walked down row C anyway. Mr Haskard's padlock. His boxes. Nothing else.
options.senior: The bucket is good at holding bytes and checking a signature; it knows nothing about leases. The database is the record of who may see which files. So the decision belongs there, at the moment someone looks, and a presigned URL should carry that decision for a few minutes, not a week. A share becomes a row you can end. It is no longer a bearer token, a pass that works for whoever holds it, that you can't call back. Uploads go straight to the bucket in parts, so a drop costs one part instead of the whole file, and the app server never carries the bytes.

options.text: Make the bucket public so photo links never expire or break, and keep retrying failed video uploads from the start.
options.part2: New buckets don't allow public access by default, so Ifor turned off the storage's block on public access, made the bucket public and left uploads as they were. Every photo now has a plain URL that never expires. We replayed the week. Mrs Kittredge's share at midnight on Thursday was just those URLs, and all 13 opens worked, the grandson's at 00:20 outside C-14 too: the armchair, the boxes, the lamp. By 01:00 the link had worked for 169 hours, and nothing would ever stop it. Ms Quist withdrew her share on Friday; the removal man opened her album on Saturday at 02:10 and Monday at 03:30 anyway. 15 opens that should have been refused. Mr Haskard's video failed four times at 551 MiB: 2,204 MiB thrown away, nothing stored. At 02:00 I locked the office. Somewhere a phone was still opening C-14.
options.senior: A public bucket is the 7-day link without the expiry. The address is the permission: anyone who holds it gets in, forever, and only moving or deleting the file takes it back. Unit numbers make keys easy to guess, so it isn't only people who were sent the link. Amazon S3, a widely used object storage service, blocks public access on new buckets by default. It recommends keeping all four block settings on unless you really need public access, such as for a public website. The inside of someone's unit, names on the boxes, is not that. And the upload is untouched: a single upload over a fading signal never finishes.

options.text: Keep the 7-day links but delete a unit's files when its lease ends, and keep retrying failed uploads from the start.
options.verdict: Gone for her, not for anyone else
options.part2: Ifor kept the 7-day links and made the app delete a unit's files when its lease ends. We replayed the week. At 00:00 on Wednesday C-14's 40 files were deleted. At midnight on Thursday the app still signed Mrs Kittredge a 7-day link, because signing checks nothing, and all 13 opens got 404 Not Found, the answer for a file that isn't there. The family chat saw nothing. On Friday her daughter rang for the photos of her father's armchair, and there was nothing to send, nor any record for us if Mrs Kittredge said we'd damaged her things. Ms Quist's lease hadn't ended, so nothing of hers was deleted: the removal man opened her album at 02:10 on Saturday and 03:30 on Monday, after she withdrew it. 2 opens that should have been refused. Mr Haskard's upload failed four times at 551 MiB, 2,204 MiB thrown away. The link found nothing, but it still never asked anyone.
options.senior: Deleting at lease end ties two separate questions together: how long files should be kept, and who may open them now. It fixed Mrs Kittredge's link only because her files were gone. It does nothing while a lease is running. Then a 7-day link is still a bearer token, a pass that works for whoever holds it, which is why Ms Quist couldn't withdraw hers. Keep files for as long as there's a stated reason, delete them on that schedule, and decide access on every look.

options.text: Stream every file through the app's server, which checks the lease on every open, and resume uploads by the part.
options.verdict: Trade-off: right, and every byte is yours
options.part2: Ifor made every photo and video go through the app server, which checks the database on each request, and made uploads go through it part by part. We replayed the week. The app refused Mrs Kittredge's share, because her lease had ended. The removal man saw Ms Quist's album at 19:30 on Thursday and was refused after she withdrew it. No open that should have been refused, none refused that should have worked. Mr Haskard's upload lost one 8 MiB part at the drop, 7 MiB thrown away. Then the busiest hour came: 400 gallery opens of about 120 MiB, 48,000 MiB through the app server in an hour, 112% of its 100 Mbps line. Pages hung, videos stalled, and tenants at the gate couldn't load their own units. Ifor says it's right, just expensive: every byte is now his to carry.
options.senior: Proxying, passing every file through your own server, puts the check in the right place, on every request. That is why every access decision came out right. But it makes the app server the pipe for every byte the bucket could have sent itself. So bandwidth, how much data the line carries, and server time grow with how much people watch. A presigned URL issued right after the same check gives the same decision. And it lets the bucket, or a CDN in front of it, carry the bytes: a CDN is a network of servers that keep copies close to viewers. Proxy only where you must see every read, such as small, very sensitive files.

sim.title: Run Prothero's storage lab
sim.lede: You're Ifor, replaying the week from Tue 22 Sep 23:00, an hour before Mrs Kittredge's lease on C-14 ends, to Thu 01 Oct 01:00, one hour a second. The events are fixed and come from the story: C-14 cleared on Wednesday at 10:00 and let to Mr Haskard at 16:00, his 612 MiB upload at 21:00, Mrs Kittredge's share at midnight on Thursday and the 13 opens of it, and Ms Quist's share with the removal man, her withdrawal on Friday at 12:00 and his three opens. Share links point either at the files, as presigned URLs signed at share time with the app's long-lived key, or at the gallery page, where the app asks the database at share time and on every open and only then signs links for that visit. Signing on its own checks nothing: not the lease, not whether the files exist. A public bucket lets anyone with a file's URL read it, with no expiry. Proxy mode checks the database on every request and sends every byte through the app server. Delete at lease end removes C-14's 40 files at 00:00 on Wednesday. Nobody should open C-14's files through a share made after its lease ended, and the removal man may open A-03's until Ms Quist withdraws it. The upload runs at 1 MiB a second; the signal holds for 551 MiB, 90 percent, then drops for 30 seconds. A single upload restarts from zero and the app gives up after 4 tries; a multipart upload keeps its finished parts and resends only the part that was in flight. With the transcode pipeline on, a stored video makes the bucket send an event to the queue 2 seconds later, and the transcoder takes 4 minutes to make 4 variant streams of 6-second segments. The busiest-hour stats count 400 gallery opens of 120 MiB through the server in proxy mode, or 0.05 MiB of page and links an open otherwise, against a 100 Mbps line. Changing any setting replays from the start, and the log describes each event as it was then. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: skip to the end as now. The C-14 link works for 168 h 0 min, 12 opens of a room that is gone, then 403 at 00:20; with the removal man's two late opens, 14 should have been refused, and Mr Haskard's upload throws away 2,204 MiB. Turn on the public bucket: 15, and the link still works at 169 h. Turn it off and delete at lease end: C-14's opens get 404 and 40 files are gone, but the removal man still gets in twice. Turn that off and try proxy mode: 0 and 0, but 48,000 MiB through the server in the busiest hour, 112% of its line. Back to links to the files, set to 5 minutes: Mrs Kittredge still sees C-14 at 00:02, and the removal man's rightful open is refused. Now share the gallery page with 5-minute links: 0 and 0, and 20 MiB on the server. Turn on multipart: 7 MiB thrown away with 8 MiB parts, 51 with 100 MiB parts. Last, turn on the transcode pipeline with multipart on, then off.

explain.oneLine: Nothing kept the room. A 7-day presigned URL, signed a day after the lease ended by an app that never asked its database, kept opening the old photos in the bucket until it expired, and nothing could call it back.

steps.title: The bucket holds the bytes; the database holds the truth.
steps.text: Object storage keeps each file whole, as an object under a key, in a bucket. Amazon S3 is Amazon's object storage service. Its guide says its data model is a flat structure, with no hierarchy of subbuckets or subfolders. The console, its web control screen, only infers folders from key prefixes, the starts of keys, such as units/C-14/. Objects are usually written and read whole over HTTP. S3 Standard, its everyday storage class, is designed for 99.999999999% durability, the chance of not losing a file, and 99.99% availability over a given year. It keeps copies on multiple devices across at least three Availability Zones, separate buildings with their own power. That makes it a good home for photos, video and backups: large, rarely changed, read whole. What it doesn't hold is meaning. Which unit a file belongs to, who rents that unit until when, and who they have shared it with are small, changing facts. You look them up and update them together, so they belong in the database. Ifor stored the files well and then let the bucket answer questions only the database could.

steps.title: A presigned URL is a permission slip anyone can carry.
steps.text: A presigned URL grants time-limited access to one object. It works in steps. First the app signs it with its own credentials, adding an expiry time. Next someone sends it to S3 as an HTTP request. Then S3 checks the signature and the expiry, at the time of that request, and sends the file if both pass. Nothing else is checked: not the lease, not who is asking. S3's guide calls presigned URLs bearer tokens that grant access to those who possess them, and says one can be used many times, up to its expiry. The limits come from the credentials. IAM, short for Identity and Access Management, is the login system of AWS, Amazon's cloud. Signed with an IAM user's key, a link can be valid for up to 7 days. Temporary credentials expire on their own, such as those of an IAM role, an identity a program takes on for a while. A link signed with them expires when they do, even if you asked for longer. For a role on an EC2 instance, a rented AWS server, that is typically 6 hours. Ifor used a long-lived IAM user key, so his 7 days held. The app signed at midnight on Thursday, a day after the lease ended, checking only the login. The link expired at 00:00 on Thursday 1 October, eight days after the lease, and worked for the 168 hours before that.

steps.title: Nothing could call it back.
steps.text: S3's guide offers no way to cancel one link. What it says is that a presigned URL expires when the credential used to create it is revoked, deleted or deactivated, even if the URL was created with a later expiration time. So the only way to stop Mrs Kittredge's link early was to kill the app's key, which would have broken every tenant's links at once. Ms Quist's withdrawn share ran on for the same reason. A bucket policy, a set of rules attached to the bucket, can refuse old signatures with the s3:signatureAge condition. S3's own example denies any presigned request whose signature is more than 10 minutes old. The lasting fix keeps the decision in the database and makes each link short. A share becomes a row in the database. Each time the gallery opens, the app reads that row and checks the lease. Only if both allow it does it sign links, and they last minutes. If the share was withdrawn or the lease has ended, no link is made.

steps.title: Uploads: in parts, straight to the bucket, then an event.
steps.text: Mr Haskard's video went up as one request, and a single upload that drops keeps nothing: four tries at 551 of 612 MiB, 2,204 MiB thrown away. A multipart upload goes in steps. First the app starts it, and S3 hands back an upload ID, a ticket number for this upload. Next the phone sends numbered parts of 5 MiB to 5 GiB each, up to 10,000 of them; a GiB is 1,024 MiB. S3 stores each part as it arrives, and a part that fails is simply sent again. Last, a complete request joins the parts in order into one object. S3 calls it a best practice for objects of 100 MB or more. It says that over a spotty network you only retry the parts that were interrupted, which makes it S3's way to do a resumable upload, one that carries on after a drop. With 8 MiB parts the drop cost part 69 alone, 7 MiB. The app can hand the phone presigned upload links, so the bytes go straight to the bucket and never through the app server. Once the object exists, S3 event notifications, short messages about what happened, can post to a queue, and a worker takes the job. They are designed to be delivered at least once, so sometimes twice, and typically arrive in seconds. So the worker must be idempotent, safe to run twice on the same file, as in The Queue Outside. And it should write its output under another prefix or bucket. Otherwise its own output lands, sends a new event, and starts the worker again.

steps.title: Video: several versions, small pieces, through a CDN.
steps.text: A phone in row C can't play a 612 MiB file over a fading signal. Transcoding makes several versions of the video at different resolutions, picture sizes, and bitrates, here Ifor's choice of 1080p, 720p, 480p and 360p. It cuts each into short media segments, 6 seconds here, listed in a media playlist. HLS is described in RFC 8216, one of the internet's published standards. It adds a master playlist that lists the variant streams, and says clients should switch between them to adapt to network conditions. Playing works in steps. The player reads the master playlist. It picks a version that suits its signal and fetches that version's playlist. Then it fetches segments one by one. If the signal weakens, it takes the next segment from a smaller version. DASH, another standard, does the same job with an MPD manifest, its own list of versions. 256 seconds of video makes 43 segments per variant stream, 177 files with the playlists. Each segment is a small file that never changes, which is what a CDN caches well, as in Mirrors Everywhere. A CDN is a network of servers that keep copies close to viewers. For private video, CloudFront, Amazon's CDN, can require its own signed URLs or signed cookies, small notes the browser carries. It recommends that users come through CloudFront rather than straight to the bucket.

diagram.aria: The fix. Phones open the unit's gallery page in the Prothero app, which asks the app database whether this person may see these files now, and only then signs links that last 5 minutes. Phones fetch files from the bucket prothero-units with those links and upload video to it in parts. Block Public Access is on. When a video lands, the bucket sends an event to a queue, a transcoder takes the job and writes 4 variant streams of 6-second segments back to the bucket. A CDN serves the HLS segments to phones, with the bucket as its origin.

explain.caption: The fix. A share is a link to the unit's gallery page. Each time it opens, the app asks the database whether this person may see these files now, and only then signs links that last 5 minutes; Mrs Kittredge's share after her lease ended is refused, and Ms Quist's ends when she withdraws it. Phones fetch files and upload video straight to the bucket, in 8 MiB parts. A finished video sends an event to the queue, and the transcoder writes 4 variant streams of 6-second segments back, served through a CDN.

fix.title: The fix: share a page, sign for minutes, upload in parts
fix.text: Make every share a row in the database: who shared which unit's files with whom, ending when the lease ends or the tenant withdraws it. A share link points at the app's gallery page. Each time the page opens, the app asks the database whether this person may see these files now, and only then signs presigned URLs that last 5 minutes for that visit. In the sim's week that refuses Mrs Kittredge's share outright, ends the removal man's access on Friday at 12:00, and lets no wrong open through. Sign with temporary credentials from a role rather than a long-lived key, so no link can outlive a few hours. Add an s3:signatureAge limit to the bucket policy as a backstop. Keep Block Public Access, S3's switch that refuses public reads, on. Upload video straight from the phone as a multipart upload in 8 MiB parts, with presigned part links. Retry only a failed part: 7 MiB thrown away instead of 2,204. Add a lifecycle rule, a bucket setting that acts after a set time, with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload, to stop uploads nobody finished. Turn on the event, queue and transcoder so each video becomes HLS variant streams served through a CDN. Decide separately how long files are kept after a lease ends, and delete them on that schedule.

limits: A signed link is still a bearer token, usable by whoever holds it, for its lifetime. Anyone who copies a 5-minute URL out of the page can use or forward it for those 5 minutes. And a download that starts before the expiry carries on, because S3 checks the expiry only when each request arrives.

Short, unique URLs usually cache badly. Each presigned URL has its own query string, the part after the ?, where the signature sits. A CDN that files its saved copies under the full address, query string included, sees every one as a new file. For video through a CDN, sign at the CDN instead, with CloudFront signed URLs or cookies, and keep the bucket closed to everyone else.

Multipart only helps if the app keeps the upload ID and its list of finished parts through a dropped connection or an app restart. Parts of uploads nobody completes are billed until they are stopped, so the lifecycle rule is part of the fix, not an extra.

head: Choice
Good
Bad
rows: Links never break for a week, and the app server carries no file bytes: 20 MiB in the busiest hour.
14 opens that should have been refused. The C-14 link worked 168 h, all after the lease ended, and Ms Quist couldn't withdraw hers.
Simplest of all, and nothing ever expires.
15 opens that should have been refused, the C-14 link still working at 169 h, for anyone who has or guesses a URL. Nothing can be withdrawn. Needs Block Public Access switched off.
C-14's link finds nothing: 13 opens get 404.
40 files gone, with them any record of the unit. The removal man still gets in twice after Ms Quist withdraws her share.
Proxy every file through the app
Every request checked: 0 opens that should have been refused, 0 rightful ones refused.
48,000 MiB through the server in the busiest hour, 112% of its 100 Mbps line. Pages hang and videos stall.
0 and 0, like the proxy, with the bytes still going straight from the bucket: 20 MiB on the server.

The app must keep the upload ID and finished parts, and unfinished parts are billed until aborted. 100 MiB parts lose 51 MiB at the same drop.

explain.seniorTake: Put bytes in object storage and meaning in the database, and never let a URL be the only record of who may see something. A presigned URL is a decision frozen at signing time and carried by whoever holds it. The only thing that kills it early is killing the key that signed it. So make the decision at the moment of each look, against the database, and let the URL live just long enough to fetch the file. Choose the lifetime by what a copied link could do in that time, not by how annoying an expired one is. An app that signs afresh on every open never shows anyone an expired link anyway. Send uploads straight from the client, the phone or browser, in parts. React to the object landing through an event and a queue. And give video several sizes in small segments behind a CDN.

realWorld.title: Amazon S3: who can create a presigned URL, and for how long
realWorld.text: S3's guide says you can use presigned URLs to grant time-limited access to objects without updating your bucket policy, and that the credentials it uses are those of whoever generated the URL. An IAM user's link is valid up to 7 days when you're using AWS Signature Version 4, AWS's current way of signing. Temporary security credentials can't be valid for longer than the credentials themselves: with IAM role credentials, the presigned URL expires when the role session expires, even if you specify a longer expiration time, and role credentials used by Amazon EC2 instances last typically 6 hours. With the S3 console, the expiration can be set between 1 minute and 12 hours. With the AWS CLI or SDKs, the command-line tool and the code libraries programs use, it can be as high as 7 days.

realWorld.title: Amazon S3: bearer tokens, checked at request time
realWorld.text: The same guide says you can use a presigned URL multiple times, up to the expiration date and time, and that presigned URLs are bearer tokens that grant access to those who possess them, so it recommends protecting them appropriately. S3 checks the expiration date and time at the time of the HTTP request: a large download that starts just before expiry continues, but if the connection drops and the client restarts after expiry, the download fails. In general, it says, a presigned URL expires when the credential you used to create it is revoked, deleted, or deactivated, even if the URL was created with a later expiration time. Its example bucket policy uses the s3:signatureAge condition to deny any presigned URL request if the signature is more than 10 minutes old.

realWorld.title: Amazon S3: uploading with a presigned URL
realWorld.text: A presigned URL can allow an upload without requiring another party to have AWS security credentials or permissions. It is limited by the permissions of the user who creates it, and if an object with the same key already exists, S3 replaces it with the uploaded object. That is how a phone can send its bytes straight to the bucket while the app only decides and signs.

realWorld.title: Amazon S3: multipart upload
realWorld.text: Multipart upload lets you upload a single object as a set of parts, and if transmission of any part fails, you can retransmit that part without affecting other parts. S3 calls it a best practice for objects that are 100 MB or larger. Over a spotty network, it says, you only need to retry uploading the parts that are interrupted, and you don't need to restart uploading your object from the beginning. It is a three-step process: initiate the upload, upload the parts, and complete it. After you initiate, there is no expiry, and you are billed for the uploaded parts until you complete or stop the upload, so S3 recommends a lifecycle rule with the AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload action.

realWorld.title: Amazon S3: multipart limits
realWorld.text: S3's limits table gives a maximum object size of 48.8 TiB, a maximum of 10,000 parts per upload, part numbers 1 to 10,000, and a part size of 5 MiB to 5 GiB, with no minimum size limit on the last part.

realWorld.title: Amazon S3: event notifications
realWorld.text: S3 can send notifications when certain events happen in a bucket, including new object created events, to Amazon SNS topics, Amazon SQS queues, AWS Lambda functions and Amazon EventBridge: AWS's services for passing on messages, holding queues, running small pieces of code and routing events. The guide says notifications are designed to be delivered at least once, typically in seconds but sometimes a minute or longer. It warns that a notification writing to the same bucket that triggers it could cause an execution loop, the worker setting itself off again and again, and suggests two buckets or a trigger that applies only to a prefix used for incoming objects.

realWorld.title: Amazon S3: Block Public Access
realWorld.text: S3's guide says that by default, new buckets and objects don't allow public access, but users can modify bucket policies or object permissions to allow it, and the four Block Public Access settings override those. AWS recommends turning on all four settings, and customizing them only if you require some level of public access, for example to host a static website.

realWorld.title: Amazon S3: keys, not folders
realWorld.text: The object key uniquely identifies the object in a bucket. The S3 data model is a flat structure: you create a bucket, and the bucket stores objects, and there is no hierarchy of subbuckets or subfolders. The console infers folders from key name prefixes and the / delimiter.

realWorld.title: Amazon S3: durability
realWorld.text: A storage class is a price and speed tier in S3. S3 Standard and most other storage classes redundantly store objects on multiple devices across a minimum of three Availability Zones in an AWS Region. S3 Standard is designed to provide 99.999999999% durability and 99.99% availability of objects over a given year.

realWorld.title: RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming, August 2017
realWorld.text: RFC 8216, by R. Pantos and W. May, describes a protocol for transferring unbounded streams of multimedia data. A Media Playlist contains a list of Media Segments, which, when played sequentially, will play the multimedia presentation. A Master Playlist provides a set of Variant Streams, each of which describes a different version of the same content, and clients should switch between different Variant Streams to adapt to network conditions. The EXT-X-TARGETDURATION tag specifies the maximum Media Segment duration. The RFC uses the word Renditions for alternate versions such as other languages or camera angles, though many tools call each bitrate version a rendition.

realWorld.title: MDN: transcoding for DASH
realWorld.text: MDN, Mozilla's reference site for web developers, has a guide. It says that if you use Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (DASH) for adaptive bitrate streaming, you need to transcode your assets into multiple resolutions, and that most DASH clients expect a Media Presentation Description (MPD) manifest file, typically generated while generating the multiple resolution files.

realWorld.title: Amazon CloudFront: private content
realWorld.text: To restrict content to selected users, CloudFront can require users to access it with special CloudFront signed URLs or signed cookies. AWS also recommends requiring CloudFront URLs rather than URLs that reach the origin, such as Amazon S3, directly, to prevent users from bypassing the restrictions in the signed URLs or cookies.

asked: Design file uploads for a photo-sharing app.
What is a presigned URL, and what are its risks?
How does video streaming adapt to bandwidth?
interview.answer: Keep files and records apart. Photos and videos go to object storage, and the database records each file's key, owner, size and who may see it. Uploads go in steps. The client asks the API, the app's front door for requests, for permission. The API checks the user and returns presigned upload links. Then the bytes go straight to the bucket. Large files use multipart upload, so a dropped connection costs one part. The client keeps the upload ID and finished parts, and a lifecycle rule aborts abandoned uploads. When the object lands, an event notification goes to a queue. Idempotent workers, safe to run twice, make thumbnails or transcode video. They write outputs under another prefix and mark the file ready in the database. A presigned URL is a time-limited permission signed with your credentials. Anyone holding it can use it until it expires. It can't be withdrawn one by one, only by revoking the signing credentials, and it can't outlive temporary credentials. So sign short-lived links at the moment an authorised user views a file. Keep the bucket private with public access blocked, and cap signature age in the bucket policy. For streaming, transcode each video into several bitrates and resolutions and cut them into short segments. Publish an HLS master playlist or a DASH manifest listing the versions. The player measures its throughput, how fast data is arriving, and switches between them, and a CDN caches the segments close to viewers.

terms.def: A building or yard of lockable rooms rented out by the month for people's belongings. Prothero Self Storage has 212 units.
One lockable room in a self-storage facility, such as C-14, with its tenant's padlock on the door.
The agreement that a tenant rents a unit from one date to another. Mrs Kittredge's lease on C-14 ended at Wed 23 Sep 00:00.
Letting a unit to a new tenant after the last one leaves. C-14 was let to Mr Haskard at 16:00 on Wednesday 23 September.
The page in the Prothero app that shows one unit's photos and videos. Only the unit's tenant can open it, unless a share lets someone else in.
Letting someone else see a unit's album. As now it hands out presigned links to the files; in the fix it is a database row the gallery page checks.
Ending a share in the app. Ms Quist withdrew hers at 12:00 on Friday 25 September; with links to the files, nothing checked that she had.
Mebibyte and gibibyte: 1,048,576 bytes and 1,024 MiB. S3 states part sizes in MiB and GiB; Mr Haskard's video is 612 MiB.
Storage that keeps each file whole, as an object under a name called a key, in a bucket, sent and fetched whole over the web. Amazon S3 is one.
A container for objects in object storage, with its own settings and policy. Ifor's is prothero-units.
One stored file in object storage, with its key and a few facts such as its size. It is replaced whole, never edited in place.
The name that identifies an object in its bucket, such as units/C-14/IMG_0412.jpg. Slashes are part of the name, not folders.
The start of a key, such as units/C-14/. Tools show prefixes as folders, and settings such as event triggers can apply to one prefix.
How unlikely it is that stored data is lost. S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% durability of objects over a given year.
A link to one object that carries a signature made with someone's credentials and an expiry time. Anyone holding it can use it until it expires.
A credential that works for whoever holds it, with no check of who they are. S3's guide calls presigned URLs bearer tokens.
AWS's current way of signing requests. A presigned URL signed with an IAM user's key and SigV4 can be valid for up to 7 days.
A named login in an AWS account's IAM, short for Identity and Access Management. It can have a long-lived access key. Ifor's app signs links with one.
A pair of an ID and a secret that a program uses to sign AWS requests. An IAM user's access key lasts until someone deactivates or deletes it.
AWS credentials that expire on their own, such as an IAM role's. A presigned URL signed with them stops working when they expire.
An AWS identity that programs take on for a while, getting temporary credentials. On an EC2 instance, a rented AWS server, they typically last about 6 hours.
The AWS Command Line Interface: a program for running AWS commands from a terminal. With it or an AWS SDK, a presigned URL can last up to 7 days.
Amazon Simple Notification Service: AWS's service that passes each message sent to a topic, a named channel, on to everything signed up to it.
Rules attached to a bucket that allow or deny requests, for example denying presigned requests whose signature is too old.
A bucket policy condition with the age of a request's signature in milliseconds. S3's example denies presigned requests signed more than 10 minutes ago.
A bucket whose policy or permissions let anyone read objects by their plain URLs, with no signature and no expiry.
Four S3 settings that override policies and permissions granting public access. New buckets don't allow public access by default; AWS recommends turning on all four.
Sending a whole file in one request. If the connection drops, nothing is stored and the upload starts again from zero.
Uploading one object as numbered parts: start it, send parts that can each be retried, then complete it so the parts are joined in order.
One numbered piece of a multipart upload, 5 MiB to 5 GiB except the last, up to 10,000 per upload. In the sim, a drop loses only the part in flight.
The identifier S3 returns when a multipart upload starts. Every part, the list of parts and the final complete request name it.
A bucket setting that acts on objects or uploads after a set time, such as deleting old files or stopping unfinished uploads.
The lifecycle action that stops multipart uploads still unfinished after a set number of days, so their parts stop being billed.
An upload that can carry on from where it stopped after a dropped connection instead of starting again. Multipart upload is S3's way to do it.
A presigned URL that allows sending one object, or one part, so a phone can send its bytes straight to the bucket without AWS credentials of its own.
A message S3 sends when something happens in a bucket, such as a new object, to a queue, a topic, a function or EventBridge. Delivered at least once.
The kind of S3 event notification sent when a new object is created, including when a multipart upload completes.
Turn a video into new versions with a different format, resolution or bitrate, here so phones on weak signal can play it.
How many bits a second a video or audio stream uses, often in kbps. A lower bitrate means a smaller, lower-quality stream.
How many lines of pixels a video frame has from top to bottom. Ifor's plan makes one version at each of these four.
HTTP Live Streaming: video cut into short files listed in playlists, sent like ordinary web pages. Described in RFC 8216, a published internet standard.
In HLS, one version of the same content at a particular bitrate, format and resolution, with its own media playlist. Many tools call it a rendition.
In RFC 8216, an alternate version such as another language or camera angle. In everyday use, often each bitrate version of a video.
One short piece of a stream, such as 6 seconds of video, fetched as its own file. 256 seconds at 6 seconds makes 43 segments.
An HLS text file listing one variant stream's media segments in order, which played one after another make the video.
An HLS text file listing the variant streams of one video, so the player can choose one and switch as the network changes.
The HLS playlist tag that gives the maximum media segment duration, such as 6 seconds.
Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP: a standard that, like HLS, offers a video at several bitrates in segments, described by an MPD manifest.
Media Presentation Description: the DASH manifest file that lists a video's versions and segments, as HLS's playlists do.
Streaming where the player switches between versions of a video at different bitrates as its connection gets better or worse.
In the sim, every file goes through the app server, which checks the database on each request and sends the bytes itself.

terms.term: CloudFront signed URL and signed cookie
terms.def: CloudFront's own time-limited permissions for private content at the CDN, used instead of S3 presigned URLs when files go through CloudFront.
An HTTP request for part of a file, by byte positions in a Range header, so a download can carry on from where it stopped.
The ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control on defining and enforcing rules for who and what may access information and other assets.
The GDPR principle that personal data is kept in a form that identifies people for no longer than its purposes need.
In the GDPR, the living person that personal data is about, such as a tenant whose name is on the boxes in a photo.
The steps that take new files in, check them and turn them into the form a system needs. LATENT a3e09 builds them for AI search.
The sim's count of opens that worked though nobody should have got in: any open of C-14's share, or the removal man's after the withdrawal.
The sim's count of opens that should have worked and didn't, such as the removal man's at 19:30 when the link had already expired.
MiB the phone sent that ended up in no stored object: every byte of a failed single upload, or the part in flight at a drop.
19:00 to 20:00 at Prothero: about 400 gallery opens of about 120 MiB each, against the app server's 100 Mbps line.

atWork: Picture a common incident. A support tool emails customers a link to download their files. To stop the tickets about broken links, someone sets the expiry to 7 days. A customer closes their account on Monday and forwards the email. On Thursday the link still downloads everything, and nobody can stop it without rotating, replacing, the key that signs every link. Look for the same in your own systems. With read-only access, search the code for presigned URLs. In the AWS SDKs, the code libraries, look for calls such as generate_presigned_url or getSignedUrl. For each one, write down its expiry, which credentials sign it, and what the code checks before signing. Look for URLs that are stored or emailed instead of made when someone clicks. Check that Block Public Access is on for every bucket, that bucket policies don't grant reads to everyone, and whether one caps s3:signatureAge. Find your large uploads. Are they single requests through your servers, or multipart straight to the bucket? And is there a lifecycle rule with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload? Your company may be pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the international standard for managing information security. Its control A.5.15 (access control) expects rules for who may access information that are defined and enforced. A link that outlives the access it was issued for is the kind of gap an auditor finds. Its control A.8.10 (information deletion) expects information to be deleted when it is no longer needed. So give files a stated retention, how long they are kept, and delete on that schedule, rather than deleting when a lease ends or never. Where the photos show personal data, such as names on boxes, the GDPR, Europe's data protection law, applies. Its Article 5(1)(e), storage limitation, asks that such data be kept in a form that identifies people for no longer than its purposes need. Build both in from the first version, not at audit time. The upload half of this case, files landing in object storage, an event, a queue and an idempotent worker, is the front of the ingestion pipelines that LATENT a3e09 builds.

recall.prompt: A climbing club's app lets members film trips in mountain huts with weak signal, upload the videos, and share albums with other members. How would you build the uploads and the sharing?

keyIdeas.idea: Upload straight from the phone to object storage, in parts that can be retried on their own
The database records who may see which files, and it is checked when someone opens an album
Short-lived presigned URLs are signed at the moment an allowed member views a file
A storage event on upload triggers processing, such as thumbnails or transcoding, through a queue

recall.model: Keep the videos in object storage and the facts in the database: each file's key, its owner, and which albums and members may see it. Uploads go in steps. The app asks the API for permission. The API checks the member and returns presigned upload links. The phone sends a multipart upload straight to the bucket, in parts of a few MiB, retrying only the part that a dropped hut signal interrupted. The phone keeps the upload ID and the finished parts so it can carry on later, and a lifecycle rule clears uploads nobody finished. When the object lands, an event notification goes to a queue. An idempotent worker, safe to run twice, makes thumbnails and transcodes the video into several bitrates for streaming. For sharing, an album share is a row in the database. When a member opens the album, the app checks that row and signs short-lived presigned URLs, a few minutes long, for that view only. Keep the bucket private with public access blocked.

recall.prompt: A support tool emails customers a 7-day link to download their account archive. On Monday a customer closes their account; on Thursday the link they forwarded to a former colleague still downloads the archive. Why does it still work, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The link is a bearer token: whoever holds it can use it until it expires, and closing the account changes nothing it checks
One link can't be withdrawn on its own; only revoking or rotating the signing credentials kills it, which breaks every link
Email a link to the app instead, which checks the account at download time and only then signs a short-lived link

recall.model: The emailed link is a presigned URL, and a presigned URL is a bearer token: whoever holds it can use it until it expires. S3 only checks the signature and the expiry. Closing the account changed a row in the database that nothing checks when the link is used. It can't be withdrawn one by one either. The only way to kill it early is to revoke or rotate the signing key, which breaks every link that key ever signed. So change what the email carries: a link to the app's own download page. When someone clicks it, the app checks the account and their access at download time. Only then does it sign a short-lived presigned URL, a few minutes long, for that download. Sign with temporary role credentials rather than a long-lived key, and add an s3:signatureAge limit to the bucket policy as a backstop.

recall.prompt: An app on an EC2 instance signs S3 presigned URLs with its instance role's temporary credentials and asks for a 7-day expiry. According to S3's guide, when does such a link stop working?
options: After 7 days, exactly as requested, whatever credentials signed it
After 12 hours, the longest any such link can last
When the role credentials expire, even though 7 days were requested
Never, until the object it points to is removed from the bucket
recall.why: S3's guide says temporary security credentials can't give a presigned URL a longer life than they have themselves: with IAM role credentials the URL expires when the role session expires, even if you specify a longer expiration time, and role credentials used by EC2 instances last typically 6 hours. The 12-hour limit applies only to links made in the S3 console; the AWS CLI and SDKs allow up to 7 days with an IAM user's key.

recall.prompt: Halfway through an HLS video, a viewer's signal drops from strong to weak. What does a well-behaved player do?
options: Switches to a lower-bitrate variant stream listed in the master playlist
Keeps downloading the same file and pauses until the signal returns
Asks the server to re-encode a smaller copy on the spot
Restarts the video from the beginning at the lowest quality
recall.why: An HLS master playlist lists variant streams, versions of the same content at different bitrates and resolutions, each cut into short segments. RFC 8216 says clients should switch between different Variant Streams to adapt to network conditions, so the player picks the next segment from a smaller version and carries on. The versions were made ahead of time, when the video was transcoded.

recall.prompt: A 612 MiB multipart upload in 8 MiB parts loses its connection while part 69 of 77 is in flight. What has to be sent again?
options: The whole 612 MiB, because the object doesn't exist until it completes
Only the last 4 MiB, which S3 always asks for first
Nothing, because S3 finishes the part from the bytes it received
Part 69 and the parts after it, since parts 1 to 68 are already stored
recall.why: S3 stores each finished part as soon as it arrives; the object only appears when the complete request joins them. If a part fails, you retransmit that part without affecting the others, so the 68 stored parts stay and the upload carries on from part 69. Here that throws away 7 MiB, against 551 MiB for every failed single upload.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Gallery pages and 5-minute links have worked all winter. Then a security review asked Ifor to stop using the long-lived key, so the app now signs with the server's role. This week tenants say the Download my whole unit button, which emails a 24-hour link to a zip file, stops working after a few hours. Mr Haskard's 3 GiB zip failed at 80 percent on the yard's signal at 22:00, and at 07:00 it wouldn't start again at all. The owner wants the long-lived key back.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why do the links die early, why won't the download start again, and what should Ifor do?

keyIdeas.idea: A presigned URL can't outlive the temporary credentials that signed it, typically about 6 hours for a role on EC2
S3 checks the expiry when each request arrives, so starting again after the link expired fails
Don't bring back the long-lived key: email a link to the app, which checks and signs a fresh short link on each click, and resume with byte ranges

coldCase.model: The links die early because a presigned URL can't outlive the credentials that signed it. The app now signs with the server's role, whose temporary credentials last typically about 6 hours, so a 24-hour link stops when they do. The download won't start again because S3 checks the expiry when each request arrives. A download that starts in time carries on, but a fresh request after the link has expired fails. Don't bring back the long-lived key; the review was right. Stop emailing links to files. Email a link to the app's download page, which checks the tenant and signs a fresh, short link each time they click, including when they come back to resume. Let the phone resume with byte ranges: a Range header, a line in the request naming the bytes it's missing, on a freshly signed link. Then a drop at 80 percent costs only what's left.
